l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: Matthew 1 opens with the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David and son of Abraham, tracing descent from Abraham through David, the exile to Babylon, and Jacob to Joseph, husband of Mary, and groups it into three sets of fourteen generations. The chapter then recounts the birth of Jesus Christ: Mary, engaged to Joseph, is found pregnant by the Holy Spirit. Joseph, a righteous man, intends to put her away secretly, but an angel of the Lord appears to him in a dream and tells him to take Mary as his wife and name her son Jesus, who will save his people from their sins. The text presents this as fulfilling the prophecy of a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel, 'God with us'. Joseph obeys, takes Mary as his wife, and names the firstborn son Jesus after his birth.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is introduced as the son of David and the son of Abraham, the one in whom the genealogy culminates, born of Mary and called Christ. He is conceived by the Holy Spirit, is to be named Jesus because he will save his people from their sins, and is called Immanuel, 'God with us'.

l: Abraham, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: Abraham stands at the head of the genealogy, becoming the father of Isaac. Jesus Christ is called his son, and the generations from Abraham to David are counted as fourteen.

l: David, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: David, called King David, is the son of Jesse and becomes the father of Solomon by her who had been Uriah's wife. Jesus Christ is called his son, and Joseph is addressed by the angel as 'son of David'. The generations from David to the exile to Babylon number fourteen.

l: Joseph, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: Joseph is the son of Jacob and the husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born. A righteous man, he intends to put Mary away secretly when she is found pregnant, but after the angel speaks to him in a dream he takes her as his wife, does not know her sexually until she gives birth, and names her firstborn son Jesus.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: Mary is the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus, who is called Christ. Engaged to Joseph, she is found pregnant by the Holy Spirit before they come together, and Joseph takes her as his wife and she gives birth to her firstborn son.

l: Holy Spirit, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: The Holy Spirit is the source of Mary's pregnancy, by whom she is found to be with child before she and Joseph come together. The angel tells Joseph that what is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit.

l: angel of the Lord, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: An angel of the Lord appears to Joseph in a dream, telling him not to be afraid to take Mary as his wife because her child is conceived of the Holy Spirit. He instructs Joseph to name the son Jesus, and Joseph does as the angel commanded.

l: genealogy of Jesus Christ, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: The genealogy is called the book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, running from Abraham through David, Solomon, and the kings of Judah to Jechoniah and the exile to Babylon, then through Shealtiel and Zerubbabel to Jacob and Joseph, husband of Mary. It is summarized as three sets of fourteen generations: Abraham to David, David to the Babylonian exile, and the exile to the Christ.

l: birth of Jesus Christ, The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew / Chapter 1
s: The birth of Jesus Christ is described as occurring after Mary's engagement to Joseph, when she is found pregnant by the Holy Spirit. It is said to fulfill the Lord's word through the prophet about a virgin bearing a son called Immanuel, and Joseph names the child Jesus after he is born.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Wise men from the east come to Jerusalem seeking the newborn King of the Jews, troubling King Herod, who learns from the chief priests and scribes that the Christ is to be born in Bethlehem. Herod secretly sends the wise men to find the child, but after worshiping Jesus and offering gifts, they are warned in a dream and return home another way. Joseph is warned by an angel to flee to Egypt with the child and Mary, while Herod, angered at being mocked, kills all the male children two years old and under in Bethlehem and its surroundings. After Herod's death, an angel tells Joseph to return, and fearing Archelaus in Judea, he settles the family in Nazareth in Galilee, fulfilling what was spoken through the prophets.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Jesus is born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of King Herod and is worshiped by the wise men, who offer him gold, frankincense, and myrrh. He is taken to Egypt by night to escape Herod, later brought back to the land of Israel, and raised in Nazareth, so that he will be called a Nazarene.

l: Herod, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: King Herod is troubled by news of the newborn King of the Jews, consults the chief priests and scribes, and secretly asks the wise men to report the child's location, claiming he wants to worship him. When mocked by the wise men's departure, he angrily has all male children two years old and under killed in Bethlehem and its surroundings, and he later dies, after which Archelaus reigns in Judea in his place.

l: wise men, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: The wise men come from the east to Jerusalem asking where the King of the Jews is born, having seen his star. They are guided to the house where the child is, worship him and offer gifts, and, warned in a dream not to return to Herod, go back to their own country another way.

l: Joseph, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Joseph is told by an angel in a dream to take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt, and he does so by night. After Herod's death he is told in a dream to return to the land of Israel, and, afraid of Archelaus and warned in another dream, he withdraws to Galilee and settles in Nazareth.

l: Mary, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Mary, called the child's mother, is seen with the young child by the wise men in the house. She is taken by Joseph to Egypt, brought back to the land of Israel, and then settled in Nazareth.

l: Bethlehem, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Bethlehem of Judea is the birthplace of Jesus and, per the prophecy the chief priests cite, the place from which a governor will come to shepherd Israel. Herod sends the wise men there, and he later has the male children of Bethlehem and its surrounding countryside killed.

l: Egypt, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Egypt is where Joseph takes the child and Mary by night to escape Herod's plan to destroy him. They stay there until Herod's death, fulfilling the words "Out of Egypt I called my son," and an angel appears to Joseph there to tell him to return.

l: Nazareth, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Nazareth is a city in the region of Galilee where Joseph, Mary, and the child come to live after returning from Egypt. This fulfills what was spoken through the prophets that he will be called a Nazarene.

l: star, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: The star is seen in the east by the wise men, who take it as a sign of the birth of the King of the Jews. It goes before them and stands over the place where the young child is, and they rejoice with exceedingly great joy upon seeing it. Herod also learns from them the exact time it appeared.

l: massacre of male children, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 2
s: Herod, angered at being mocked by the wise men, sends out and kills all the male children two years old and under in Bethlehem and the surrounding countryside, based on the exact time he learned from the wise men. This is said to fulfill Jeremiah's words about a voice heard in Ramah, with Rachel weeping for her children who are no more.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: John the Baptizer preaches in the wilderness of Judea, calling people to repent because the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand, and is identified as the voice Isaiah the prophet spoke of. People from Jerusalem, Judea, and the Jordan region go out to be baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins. When Pharisees and Sadducees come, John rebukes them, warns of coming wrath, and says one mightier than he will baptize in the Holy Spirit and judge like a farmer clearing a threshing floor. Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized; John objects, but Jesus says it fulfills all righteousness and John consents. After the baptism the heavens open, the Spirit of God descends on Jesus like a dove, and a voice from the heavens calls him beloved Son.

l: John the Baptizer, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: John comes preaching in the wilderness of Judea, calling for repentance, and is identified as the one Isaiah spoke of. He wears camel's hair clothing with a leather belt, eats locusts and wild honey, baptizes people in the Jordan, and rebukes the Pharisees and Sadducees. He announces a mightier one coming after him, then baptizes Jesus after first objecting.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: Jesus comes from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. He tells John to allow it as the fitting way to fulfill all righteousness. After he comes up from the water, the Spirit of God descends on him and a voice from the heavens calls him beloved Son, with whom it is well pleased.

l: Jordan, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: The Jordan is where people from Jerusalem, Judea, and the surrounding region are baptized by John while confessing their sins. It is also where Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized, and where the heavens open over him.

l: Pharisees and Sadducees, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: Many Pharisees and Sadducees come to John for his baptism. John calls them offspring of vipers, asks who warned them to flee the coming wrath, and tells them to produce fruit worthy of repentance and not to rely on having Abraham as father.

l: people from Jerusalem, Judea, and the Jordan region, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: People from Jerusalem, all of Judea, and the region around the Jordan go out to John. They are baptized by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins.

l: baptism, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: John baptizes people in the Jordan in water for repentance, with confession of sins. He says the one coming after him will baptize in the Holy Spirit. Jesus is baptized by John, and the heavens open afterward.

l: repentance, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: John's message is "Repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand!" He tells the Pharisees and Sadducees to produce fruit worthy of repentance, warning that trees not producing good fruit are cut down and cast into the fire. His water baptism is described as being for repentance.

l: Holy Spirit, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: After Jesus is baptized and comes up from the water, he sees the Spirit of God descending as a dove and coming on him.

l: voice from the heavens, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 3
s: After Jesus's baptism, a voice out of the heavens says, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where after fasting forty days and nights he is tempted three times by the devil and answers each time with Scripture. After the devil leaves and angels serve him, Jesus hears that John was delivered up and withdraws to Galilee, settling in Capernaum in fulfillment of Isaiah's prophecy of light for those in darkness. He begins preaching, 'Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.' By the sea of Galilee he calls the brothers Simon Peter and Andrew, and then James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who immediately leave their nets, boat, and father to follow him. Jesus then goes throughout Galilee teaching, preaching, and healing, and great multitudes from many regions follow him.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness, fasts forty days and nights, and resists the devil's three temptations by quoting Scripture. After John is delivered up, he withdraws to Galilee and lives in Capernaum, begins preaching repentance, calls four fishermen to follow him, and goes about Galilee teaching, preaching, and healing, drawing great multitudes.

l: Satan, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: The devil, called the tempter, tempts Jesus to turn stones into bread, to throw himself from the temple pinnacle, and to worship him in exchange for all the kingdoms of the world. Jesus rebukes him as Satan, and the devil leaves him.

l: temptation of Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: After fasting forty days and nights and becoming hungry, Jesus is tempted three times: to command stones to become bread, to throw himself down from the temple pinnacle, and to worship the devil for all the kingdoms of the world. He answers each with 'It is written' and a quotation from Scripture, and the devil then leaves while angels come and serve him.

l: Galilee, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Jesus withdraws into Galilee after hearing John was delivered up, and Isaiah's words about 'Galilee of the Gentiles' are cited as fulfilled, with light dawning on those who sat in darkness. He calls his first disciples by its sea and goes about all Galilee teaching, preaching, and healing, and multitudes from Galilee follow him.

l: Capernaum, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Leaving Nazareth, Jesus comes and lives in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali. His settling there is presented as fulfilling what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet.

l: Kingdom of Heaven, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Jesus begins to preach that the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand and calls people to repent. His preaching is described as the Good News of the Kingdom, which he proclaims in the synagogues of Galilee.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Simon, called Peter, is seen by Jesus casting a net into the sea of Galilee with his brother Andrew, for they were fishermen. Jesus says he will make them fishers for men, and Simon immediately leaves his nets and follows him.

l: Andrew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Andrew, brother of Simon Peter, is a fisherman casting a net into the sea of Galilee when Jesus sees him. Called to come after Jesus and become a fisher for men, he immediately leaves his nets and follows.

l: James, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: James, son of Zebedee, is in a boat with his father Zebedee and his brother John, mending nets, when Jesus sees and calls him. He immediately leaves the boat and his father and follows Jesus.

l: John, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: John, brother of James and son of Zebedee, is mending nets in the boat with his father when Jesus calls him. He immediately leaves the boat and his father and follows Jesus.

l: call of the first disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Walking by the sea of Galilee, Jesus calls two pairs of fishermen brothers: Simon Peter and Andrew, then James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Jesus tells the first pair to come after him and he will make them fishers for men, and both pairs immediately leave their nets, and in the second case their boat and father, to follow him.

l: Jesus' healing ministry, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 4
s: Jesus goes about all Galilee healing every disease and sickness among the people, and the report of him spreads into all Syria. People bring him the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and torments, the demon-possessed, epileptics, and paralytics, and he heals them, while great multitudes from Galilee, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and beyond the Jordan follow him.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: In Chapter 5, Jesus sees the multitudes, goes up a mountain, and teaches his disciples who come to him. He opens with the Beatitudes, blessing the poor in spirit, mourners, the gentle, the merciful, the pure in heart, peacemakers, and the persecuted, and tells his hearers they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. He declares that he came to fulfill the law and the prophets, not destroy them, and that righteousness must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees. He then contrasts what was said to the ancient ones with his own teaching on murder and anger, adultery and lust, divorce, oaths, and retaliation. He ends by commanding love of enemies, grounded in the example of the Father in heaven, and calls his hearers to be perfect as the Father is perfect.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus goes up onto the mountain, sits, and teaches his disciples, blessing the poor in spirit, the meek, the persecuted, and others. He says he came to fulfill the law and the prophets, not to destroy them, and repeatedly contrasts what was said to the ancient ones with 'But I tell you.' He commands reconciliation, no oaths, non-resistance, and love of enemies, and calls his hearers to be perfect like the Father.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: The disciples come to Jesus after he sits down on the mountain, and he opens his mouth to teach them. They are told they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world, and that they should let their light shine so people see their good works and glorify the Father.

l: Kingdom of Heaven, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: The Kingdom of Heaven belongs to the poor in spirit and to those persecuted for righteousness' sake. Those who break the least commandments and teach others to do so will be called least in it, while those who do and teach them will be called great. No one enters it unless their righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees.

l: Beatitudes, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Verses 3-10 give a series of blessings: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and the persecuted. Each is paired with a promise, such as comfort, inheriting the earth, mercy, seeing God, and being called children of God. Verses 11-12 extend the blessing to those reproached and persecuted for Jesus's sake, who are told to rejoice because their reward in heaven is great.

l: God, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: God is described as the one who will be seen by the pure in heart and whose children the peacemakers are called. Heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool, and Jerusalem is the city of the great King. As the Father in heaven, he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the just and the unjust, and he is perfect.

l: law, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus states he did not come to destroy the law or the prophets but to fulfill them. Not the smallest letter or pen stroke will pass from the law until all things are accomplished. Breaking even the least commandments and teaching others to do so makes one least in the Kingdom, and Jesus then reinterprets several commands from the law.

l: righteousness, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled, and those persecuted for righteousness' sake are blessed. Jesus says the righteousness of his hearers must exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees for them to enter the Kingdom of Heaven.

l: murder and anger, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus cites the command 'You shall not murder' and the danger of judgment for murder. He extends it to anger at a brother without cause, saying 'Raca!' or 'You fool!', each bringing danger of the judgment, the council, or the fire of Gehenna. He instructs that one should leave a gift at the altar and first be reconciled with a brother, and should settle quickly with an adversary to avoid prison.

l: adultery and lust, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus cites 'You shall not commit adultery' and says that anyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery in his heart. He says it is more profitable to lose an eye or a hand that causes stumbling than for the whole body to be cast into Gehenna.

l: divorce, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus recalls the saying that whoever puts away his wife should give her a writing of divorce. He teaches that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

l: oaths, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus recalls the instruction not to make false vows but to perform vows to the Lord. He tells his hearers not to swear at all, whether by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or their own head. Their 'Yes' should be 'Yes' and their 'No' 'No,' since anything more is of the evil one.

l: retaliation, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus quotes 'An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth' and replaces it with a teaching not to resist the one who is evil. He instructs turning the other cheek, giving one's cloak as well as one's coat, going two miles when compelled to go one, and giving to those who ask or wish to borrow.

l: love of enemies, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 5
s: Jesus contrasts the saying 'love your neighbor and hate your enemy' with a command to love enemies, bless those who curse, do good to those who hate, and pray for persecutors. This makes his hearers children of the Father, who gives sun and rain to all. He notes that loving only those who love you, or greeting only friends, is what even tax collectors do, and concludes that his hearers should be perfect as the Father is perfect.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: In Chapter 6 the speaker instructs his listeners to practice charitable giving, prayer, and fasting in secret rather than to be seen by people, contrasting them with the hypocrites who seek glory from men and have already received their reward. He gives a model prayer beginning 'Our Father in heaven' and teaches that the Father's forgiveness depends on forgiving others. He then tells them to lay up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, warns that one cannot serve both God and Mammon, and describes the eye as the lamp of the body. Finally he urges them not to be anxious about food, drink, or clothing, pointing to the birds and lilies as evidence of the heavenly Father's care, and to seek God's Kingdom and his righteousness first.

l: God, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: The Father sees in secret and rewards openly those who give, pray, and fast without display. He knows what people need before they ask, feeds the birds, clothes the grass of the field, and knows his people need food, drink, and clothing. He forgives those who forgive others and will not forgive those who do not, and is not to be served alongside Mammon.

l: evil and adulterous generation, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: The hypocrites sound a trumpet when giving, stand and pray in synagogues and street corners to be seen, and disfigure their faces when fasting. They do these things to gain glory from men, and the text says they have already received their reward.

l: charitable giving, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: Charitable giving, called merciful deeds, is not to be done before men to be seen by them, or no reward comes from the Father. It should be done so secretly that the left hand does not know what the right does, and the Father who sees in secret will reward it openly.

l: prayer, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: Prayer is not to be performed to be seen, but done in an inner room with the door shut to the Father who is in secret. It should avoid vain repetitions as the Gentiles use, since the Father knows needs before they are asked.

l: Lord's Prayer, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: The prayer is introduced with 'Pray like this' and addresses 'Our Father in heaven.' It asks that his name be kept holy, his Kingdom come and will be done on earth as in heaven, for daily bread, forgiveness of debts as we forgive debtors, and deliverance from temptation and the evil one, ending with 'For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.'

l: fasting, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: Fasting is not to be done with a sad, disfigured face like the hypocrites, who want to be seen fasting. Instead one should anoint the head and wash the face so that only the Father, who sees in secret, knows, and he will reward it.

l: forgiveness, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: Forgiveness appears in the prayer, 'Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.' The text then states that if people forgive others their trespasses the heavenly Father will forgive them, but if they do not, neither will the Father forgive their trespasses.

l: treasure, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: Listeners are told not to lay up treasures on earth, where moth and rust consume and thieves steal, but to lay up treasures in heaven, where these cannot destroy or take them. The text says where one's treasure is, there the heart will be also.

l: anxiety, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: Listeners are told not to be anxious about life, food, drink, body, clothing, or tomorrow. The text argues that life is more than food, that anxiety cannot add a moment to one's lifespan, and that the Father who feeds birds and clothes lilies will care for them; the Gentiles seek these things, and each day's own evil is sufficient.

l: God's Kingdom, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 6
s: The Kingdom is prayed for in the model prayer ('Let your Kingdom come') and is declared to belong to the Father along with the power and glory. Listeners are told to seek it first along with his righteousness, and all their needs will then be given to them as well.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: In Chapter 7, Jesus teaches the multitudes about judging others, prayer, the way of life, and obedience. He warns against judging, using the image of a speck and a beam in the eye, and tells hearers not to give holy things to dogs or pearls to pigs. He urges asking, seeking, and knocking, assuring that the Father in heaven gives good things, and gives the rule to do to others what one wants done to oneself. He contrasts the narrow gate with the broad way, warns of false prophets known by their fruits, and says that saying 'Lord, Lord' is not enough without doing the Father's will. He closes with the wise man who built on the rock and the foolish man who built on the sand, and the multitudes are astonished because he taught with authority, unlike the scribes.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: Jesus teaches the multitudes about judging, asking, the narrow gate, false prophets, and doing God's will. He says he will tell those who work iniquity, 'I never knew you. Depart from me.' When he finishes, the multitudes are astonished because he taught with authority, not like the scribes.

l: God, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: The Father in heaven is said to give good things to those who ask him, far more than evil human parents give good gifts to their children. Entering the Kingdom of Heaven requires doing the will of this Father.

l: judging others, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: Jesus commands not to judge, so as not to be judged, and says people will be judged and measured by the same measure they use. He illustrates this with the speck in a brother's eye and the beam in one's own, calling the one who ignores his own beam a hypocrite who must first remove it to see clearly.

l: narrow gate and broad way, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: Jesus tells his hearers to enter by the narrow gate, since the wide gate and broad way lead to destruction and many enter by it. The gate and way to life are narrow and restricted, and few find it.

l: false prophets, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: Jesus warns to beware of false prophets, who come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravening wolves. They are to be known by their fruits.

l: trees and fruit, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: Jesus says people do not gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles, and that a good tree produces good fruit while a corrupt tree produces evil fruit. A tree that does not grow good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire, so by their fruits people are known.

l: those who say 'Lord, Lord', The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: Jesus says not everyone who calls him 'Lord, Lord' will enter the Kingdom of Heaven, but only the one who does the Father's will. Many will say they prophesied, cast out demons, and did mighty works in his name, yet he will tell them he never knew them and to depart, workers of iniquity.

l: wise man, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: The wise man is likened to everyone who hears Jesus's words and does them. He built his house on the rock, and it did not fall when rain, floods, and wind beat on it.

l: foolish man, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: The foolish man is likened to everyone who hears Jesus's words and does not do them. He built his house on the sand, and it fell when the storm came, and its fall was great.

l: house on the rock, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: The house on the rock was struck by rain, floods, and winds but did not fall, because it was founded on the rock. It represents the life of one who hears and does Jesus's words.

l: house on the sand, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: The house on the sand was beaten by rain, floods, and winds and fell, and its fall was great. It represents the life of one who hears Jesus's words and does not do them.

l: Jesus's teaching, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 7
s: Jesus's teaching in this unit covers not judging, asking and receiving, the golden rule, the narrow way, discerning false prophets, and doing his words rather than only hearing them. The multitudes were astonished at it because he taught with authority and not like the scribes.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: After coming down from the mountain, Jesus is followed by great multitudes and cleanses a leper by touch, telling him to show himself to the priest. In Capernaum he agrees to heal a centurion's paralyzed servant, and the centurion's confidence in Jesus' word leads Jesus to praise his faith and heal the servant. Jesus then heals Peter's wife's mother of a fever and, that evening, casts out spirits and heals all the sick, which is said to fulfill Isaiah's words. He answers a scribe and another disciple about the cost of following him, calms a violent storm on the sea for his frightened disciples, and in the country of the Gergesenes sends demons from two possessed men into a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea, after which the city begs him to leave.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: Jesus cleanses a leper, heals a centurion's servant, Peter's wife's mother, and many sick people, and casts out spirits with a word. He tells would-be followers that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, calms the storm, and sends demons into pigs, after which the city asks him to depart from their borders.

l: leper, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: A leper comes to Jesus, worships him, and says that if Jesus wants to, he can make him clean. Jesus touches him and says "Be made clean," and his leprosy is immediately cleansed; Jesus tells him to tell nobody, show himself to the priest, and offer the gift Moses commanded.

l: centurion, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: In Capernaum a centurion asks Jesus for help for his paralyzed, tormented servant, and says he is not worthy to have Jesus come under his roof, since a word will suffice, as he himself is a man under authority. Jesus marvels, says he has not found such great faith even in Israel, and tells him it will be done as he believed, and the servant is healed in that hour.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: The disciples follow Jesus into a boat, and when the storm threatens to cover it they wake the sleeping Jesus, crying "Save us, Lord! We are dying!" Jesus calls them people of little faith and calms the sea, and the men marvel that even wind and sea obey him.

l: storm at sea, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: A violent storm comes up on the sea so that the boat is covered with waves while Jesus sleeps. Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea, and there is a great calm.

l: possessed men of the Gergesenes, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: Two men possessed by demons meet Jesus in the country of the Gergesenes, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that nobody could pass that way. The demons within them are cast out by Jesus' command.

l: demons, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: The demons in the two men cry out to Jesus as Son of God and ask whether he has come to torment them before the time. They beg to be sent into the herd of pigs, and when Jesus says "Go!" they come out and enter the pigs.

l: herd of pigs, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: A large herd of pigs is feeding far from the possessed men. When the demons enter them, the whole herd rushes down the cliff into the sea and dies in the water.

l: city, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: Those who fed the pigs flee into the city and report everything, including what happened to the possessed men. All the city then comes out to meet Jesus and, on seeing him, begs him to depart from their borders.

l: healing of the sick, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 8
s: Jesus heals the leper, the centurion's servant, and Peter's wife's mother, and in the evening heals all who are sick among those brought to him. This is said to fulfill Isaiah's words, "He took our infirmities and bore our diseases."

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: Jesus crosses into his own city, where he forgives and heals a paralyzed man, prompting scribes to accuse him of blasphemy while the crowds glorify God. He calls Matthew, a tax collector, and eats with tax collectors and sinners, answering the Pharisees' criticism and John's disciples' question about fasting with sayings about physicians, mercy, the bridegroom, and new wine in fresh wineskins. A ruler asks him to restore his dead daughter; on the way a woman with a twelve-year discharge of blood touches his garment and is made well, and Jesus then raises the girl by taking her hand. He gives sight to two blind men according to their faith, and a mute demon-possessed man speaks after the demon is cast out, while the Pharisees say he casts out demons by the prince of the demons. Jesus goes through the cities and villages teaching and healing, feels compassion for the harassed multitudes, and tells his disciples to pray for laborers for the harvest.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: Jesus forgives a paralytic's sins and heals him, calls Matthew, eats with tax collectors and sinners, and answers the Pharisees and John's disciples with sayings about physicians, mercy, the bridegroom, and new wine. He heals the woman with the discharge of blood, raises the ruler's daughter, restores sight to two blind men, and casts a demon out of a mute man. He teaches and heals in all the cities and villages, is moved with compassion for the multitudes, and asks his disciples to pray for laborers for the harvest.

l: paralytic (man brought to Jesus), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: A paralyzed man lying on a bed is brought to Jesus, who, seeing the faith of those bringing him, tells him his sins are forgiven. Jesus then tells him to get up, take his mat, and go home, and he rises and departs to his house.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: The Pharisees ask Jesus' disciples why their teacher eats with tax collectors and sinners, and John's disciples say they fast often along with the Pharisees. After the mute man speaks, the Pharisees claim that Jesus casts out demons by the prince of the demons.

l: ruler, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: A ruler comes and worships Jesus, telling him that his daughter has just died and asking him to come lay his hand on her so that she will live. Jesus gets up and follows him to his house.

l: ruler's daughter, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: The ruler's daughter has just died when her father asks Jesus to come. Jesus says she is sleeping, not dead, and after the crowd is sent out he takes her by the hand and she arises, and the report spreads through the land.

l: woman with discharge of blood, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: A woman who has had a discharge of blood for twelve years comes up behind Jesus and touches the fringe of his garment, saying within herself that this will make her well. Jesus turns, calls her daughter, tells her to cheer up because her faith has made her well, and she is made well from that hour.

l: two blind men, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: Two blind men follow Jesus calling out for mercy as the son of David, and in the house they tell him yes when he asks if they believe he is able to do this. He touches their eyes and says it will be done according to their faith, and their eyes are opened. Despite his strict command to tell no one, they spread his fame throughout the land.

l: forgiveness of sins, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 9
s: Jesus declares the paralytic's sins forgiven, which leads some scribes to say he blasphemes. Jesus says he heals the man so that they may know the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, and the multitudes glorify God for giving such authority to men.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 10
s: Jesus calls his twelve disciples, gives them authority over unclean spirits and every disease, and names the twelve apostles, ending with Judas Iscariot who betrayed him. He sends them out to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, not to Gentiles or Samaritans, to preach that the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand, heal, and cast out demons, taking no money or supplies and relying on worthy households. He warns that they will be sent as sheep among wolves, delivered to councils, governors and kings, hated, and betrayed by family, but that the Spirit of their Father will speak through them and those who endure will be saved. He tells them not to fear, since the Father knows every sparrow and hair, and says those who confess him will be confessed before the Father while those who deny him will be denied. He declares he came with a sword, demands love for him above family and taking up one's cross, and promises rewards to those who receive his disciples, even with a cup of cold water.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 10
s: Jesus calls the twelve disciples, gives them authority over unclean spirits and disease, and sends them out with detailed instructions to preach, heal, and go only to the lost sheep of Israel. He warns them of persecution, tells them not to fear, says he came to send a sword rather than peace, and demands that he be loved above family. He promises that receiving his disciples is receiving him and the one who sent him.

l: twelve disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 10
s: The twelve are named: Simon called Peter, Andrew, James son of Zebedee, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew the tax collector, James son of Alphaeus, Lebbaeus called Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him. They are given authority over unclean spirits and every disease and are sent out to preach, heal, and cast out demons without money, bag, extra coats, sandals, or staff. They are told to expect hatred, trials, and betrayal, to speak openly without fear, and to flee persecution from city to city.

l: Israel, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 10
s: The house of Israel is described as lost sheep, and the disciples are sent only to it, not to Gentiles or Samaritan cities. Jesus says the disciples will not have gone through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man has come.

l: God, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 10
s: The Father is the one whose Spirit will speak in the disciples when they are delivered up, so they need not be anxious about what to say. He knows every sparrow that falls and has numbered the hairs of their heads. Jesus says he will confess before the Father those who confess him and deny those who deny him, and that receiving Jesus is receiving the one who sent him.

l: persecution of the disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 10
s: Jesus predicts the disciples will be sent as sheep among wolves, scourged in synagogues, brought before governors and kings, and hated by all for his name's sake. Family members will deliver one another to death. They are told to flee from city to city, not to fear those who kill the body, and that those who endure to the end will be saved.

l: reward for receiving disciples, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 10
s: Jesus teaches that whoever receives the disciples receives him and the one who sent him. Those who receive a prophet or righteous man as such will receive that person's reward, and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to a disciple will in no way lose his reward. Worthy households that welcome the disciples receive their peace, while those who reject them face a judgment worse than Sodom and Gomorrah.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: After finishing his instructions to the twelve disciples, Jesus goes to teach and preach in their cities. John, imprisoned, sends two disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who is to come, and Jesus answers by pointing to his works and then praises John to the crowds as a prophet and more than a prophet, identifying him as Elijah and the messenger foretold. Jesus compares this generation to children who complain that no one responds to their flute or mourning, since they rejected both John and the Son of Man. He denounces Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum for not repenting despite his mighty works, saying Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom will fare more tolerably in judgment. He thanks the Father for revealing things to infants, declares that all things are delivered to him, and invites the weary and burdened to come to him, take his yoke, and find rest.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus finishes instructing the twelve and goes to teach and preach in their cities. He answers John's question by pointing to the healing and good news happening, praises John to the crowds, denounces unrepentant cities, thanks the Father, and says all things are delivered to him and that only he can reveal the Father. He then invites the weary to come to him, describing himself as gentle and humble in heart.

l: John the Baptizer, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: John, in prison, hears of Christ's works and sends two disciples to ask whether Jesus is the one who comes. Jesus calls him a prophet and more, the messenger foretold who prepares the way, and says none born of women is greater, though the least in the Kingdom of Heaven is greater. Jesus also says John is Elijah who is to come, and that people dismissed him as having a demon because he came neither eating nor drinking.

l: this generation, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus compares this generation to children in the marketplaces who complain that their companions neither danced to the flute nor lamented at mourning. It rejected John for his fasting, saying he had a demon, and rejected the Son of Man for eating and drinking, calling him a glutton and drunkard and a friend of tax collectors and sinners.

l: Kingdom of Heaven, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus says that from the days of John the Baptizer until now the Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence and the violent take it by force. He also says that the least in the Kingdom is greater than John, who is the greatest among those born of women.

l: God, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus thanks the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, for hiding these things from the wise and understanding and revealing them to infants, because that was well-pleasing in his sight. Jesus says the Father has delivered all things to him, and that no one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

l: Chorazin, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus pronounces woe on Chorazin because it did not repent despite his mighty works done there. He says that if those works had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes, so Tyre and Sidon will find judgment more tolerable than Chorazin.

l: Bethsaida, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus pronounces woe on Bethsaida for failing to repent despite the mighty works done in it. He says Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen those works, and will have a more tolerable day of judgment than Bethsaida.

l: Capernaum, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus addresses Capernaum as exalted to heaven and says it will go down to Hades. He says that had the mighty works done there been done in Sodom, Sodom would have remained until today, and that the land of Sodom will have a more tolerable judgment than Capernaum.

l: mighty works (Jesus' mighty works), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus' works, including the blind seeing, the lame walking, lepers cleansed, the deaf hearing, the dead raised, and good news preached to the poor, are what he cites in answer to John. Most of them were done in the cities that did not repent, which Jesus denounces, saying that Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom would have responded to them.

l: those who labor and are heavily burdened, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus invites all who labor and are heavily burdened to come to him, promising to give them rest. He tells them to take his yoke and learn from him, and says they will find rest for their souls.

l: rest, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus promises rest to all who labor and are heavily burdened if they come to him. He says that by taking his yoke and learning from him, they will find rest for their souls.

l: yoke (Jesus' yoke), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 11
s: Jesus tells the weary to take his yoke upon them and learn from him, because he is gentle and humble in heart. He says his yoke is easy and his burden is light.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: In Chapter 12, Jesus is challenged by the Pharisees when his hungry disciples pluck grain on the Sabbath, and he defends them by citing David, the priests, and mercy, declaring himself Lord of the Sabbath. He then heals a man with a withered hand in a synagogue, after which the Pharisees conspire to destroy him, and he withdraws and heals the multitudes, which is said to fulfill Isaiah's prophecy of the chosen servant. After he heals a blind and mute possessed man, the Pharisees claim he casts out demons by Beelzebul, and Jesus answers with warnings about divided kingdoms, blasphemy against the Spirit, and the fruit of words. When scribes and Pharisees ask for a sign, he points to the sign of Jonah and warns of the return of an unclean spirit. Finally, when his mother and brothers wait outside, he says that whoever does the will of his Father in heaven is his brother, sister, and mother.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: Jesus defends his disciples' plucking of grain on the Sabbath, heals a man's withered hand, and withdraws when the Pharisees conspire against him. He heals a possessed blind and mute man, rebuts the charge that he acts by Beelzebul, and refuses the scribes and Pharisees a sign except that of Jonah. He declares himself Lord of the Sabbath, greater than the temple, Jonah, and Solomon, and names those who do his Father's will as his family.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: The Pharisees accuse Jesus's disciples of unlawful Sabbath work, ask whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful in order to accuse him, and then conspire to destroy him. They attribute his casting out of demons to Beelzebul, and together with certain scribes ask him for a sign. Jesus calls them offspring of vipers and an evil and adulterous generation.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: Jesus's disciples, hungry, pluck and eat heads of grain in the grain fields on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees call this unlawful. Jesus defends them as guiltless. Later he stretches his hand toward them and calls them his mother and brothers.

l: Sabbath, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: The Sabbath is the occasion of two disputes: the disciples' plucking of grain and the healing of the withered hand. Jesus argues that the priests profane it and are guiltless, that a man is worth more than a sheep, and that it is lawful to do good on it. He declares that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.

l: man with a withered hand, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: The man with a withered hand is in the synagogue when the Pharisees ask whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful. Jesus tells him to stretch out his hand, and it is restored whole like the other.

l: possessed man, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: A man possessed by a demon, blind and mute, is brought to Jesus. Jesus heals him so that he both speaks and sees, and the multitudes are amazed and ask whether Jesus is the son of David.

l: demons, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: Demons are cast out by Jesus, whom the Pharisees say does so by Beelzebul, prince of the demons. Jesus says he does it by the Spirit of God, showing that God's Kingdom has come. He also describes an unclean spirit that leaves a man, returns, and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself.

l: Beelzebul, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 12
s: Beelzebul is named by the Pharisees as the prince of the demons, by whom they claim Jesus casts out demons. Jesus replies that Satan casting out Satan would be a divided kingdom that cannot stand.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus sits by the sea and teaches the gathered multitudes in parables, beginning with a farmer whose seed falls on four kinds of ground. When the disciples ask why he uses parables, he says the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven are given to them but not to the crowds, and he explains the sower parable. He then tells parables of the darnel weeds, the mustard seed, the yeast, the hidden treasure, the pearl, and the dragnet, and privately explains the darnel parable to the disciples as a picture of the end of the age. After asking the disciples whether they understood and hearing 'Yes, Lord,' Jesus goes to his own country, where the people in the synagogue are astonished and offended by him, and he does few mighty works there because of their unbelief.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus sits by the sea and teaches the multitudes in parables, then explains the sower and darnel parables privately to his disciples. He tells further parables of the mustard seed, yeast, treasure, pearl and dragnet, and in his own country he is rejected, saying a prophet is not without honor except in his own country and house.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: The disciples ask why Jesus speaks in parables and are told the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven are given to them, and that their eyes and ears are blessed. They receive explanations of the sower and darnel parables, and answer 'Yes, Lord' when Jesus asks if they have understood.

l: multitudes (crowds around Jesus), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Great multitudes gather to Jesus by the sea, standing on the beach while he teaches from a boat. He speaks to them only in parables, and then sends them away.

l: farmer (parable of the sower), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: A farmer goes out to sow seed, which falls on the roadside, rocky ground, among thorns, and on good soil. In Jesus's account, the farmer's sowing illustrates how people hear the word of the Kingdom.

l: parable of the sower, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus tells of seed that is devoured by birds, scorched for lack of root, choked by thorns, or yields thirty, sixty or one hundred times on good soil. He explains that these are people who hear the word and fail to understand, fall away under persecution, are choked by cares and riches, or understand and bear fruit.

l: seeds (sown by the farmer), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: The seeds fall on four kinds of ground, with different outcomes: eaten, withered, choked, or fruitful. Jesus explains that they represent the word of the Kingdom sown in the hearts of those who hear.

l: parables (Jesus's teaching method), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus speaks to the multitudes only in parables, and explains to the disciples that this is because the crowds see and hear without understanding, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy. The chapter also presents it as fulfilling the saying 'I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world.'

l: Kingdom of Heaven, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus likens the Kingdom of Heaven to a field with good seed and darnel, a mustard seed that becomes a tree, yeast in meal, hidden treasure, a valuable pearl, and a dragnet. These images show it growing from small beginnings, being worth giving up everything for, and involving a final separation of the righteous from the wicked.

l: man with the wheat field (parable of the darnel), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: The man sows good seed in his field, and an enemy sows darnel among the wheat while people sleep. He tells his servants not to uproot the darnel, so the wheat is not harmed, and says he will have the reapers gather the darnel to burn and the wheat into his barn at harvest.

l: parable of the darnel weeds, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus tells of an enemy sowing darnel among wheat, with both left to grow together until harvest. He later explains to the disciples that the sower is the Son of Man, the field the world, the good seeds the children of the Kingdom, the darnel the children of the evil one, and the enemy the devil.

l: harvest (end of the age), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus explains that the harvest is the end of the age and the reapers are angels. The angels will gather out of the Kingdom all that causes stumbling and those who do iniquity and cast them into the furnace of fire, while the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's Kingdom.

l: Jesus's home country, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: Jesus comes into his own country and teaches in the synagogue there. He does not do many mighty works there because of the people's unbelief.

l: people of Jesus's country, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 13
s: The people are astonished at Jesus's wisdom and mighty works but question where he got them, noting that he is the carpenter's son and naming his mother Mary and his brothers James, Joses, Simon and Judas, along with his sisters. They are offended by him.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus and says he is John the Baptizer risen from the dead, recalling that he had imprisoned John for condemning his taking of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife. At Herod's birthday, Herodias's daughter dances, Herod swears to give her what she asks, and prompted by her mother she requests John's head on a platter; Herod, grieved but bound by his oaths, has John beheaded in prison. John's disciples bury the body and tell Jesus, who withdraws by boat, but the crowds follow him on foot and he heals their sick. Jesus feeds about five thousand men, plus women and children, with five loaves and two fish, leaving twelve baskets of leftovers. He then sends the disciples ahead by boat, prays alone on the mountain, and comes to them walking on the sea, where Peter walks toward him, begins to sink, and is saved; the wind ceases, the disciples worship him as the Son of God, and at Gennesaret all who touch his garment's fringe are made whole.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Jesus withdraws by boat to a deserted place after hearing of John's death, heals the sick among the following crowds, and feeds about five thousand men plus women and children with five loaves and two fish. He then prays alone on the mountain, walks on the sea to his disciples, saves the sinking Peter, and is worshiped as the Son of God. At Gennesaret, all who touch the fringe of his garment are made whole.

l: Herod the tetrarch, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Herod hears the report about Jesus and says to his servants that this is John the Baptizer risen from the dead. He had arrested and imprisoned John for the sake of Herodias, wanted to kill him but feared the multitude, and then, bound by an oath made at his birthday, grievedly commanded that John be beheaded. He is also called the king in the account.

l: John the Baptizer, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: John had been arrested, bound, and imprisoned by Herod after telling him it was not lawful to have Herodias, his brother Philip's wife. The multitude counted him as a prophet. He is beheaded in prison, and his disciples bury his body and tell Jesus.

l: Herodias, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Herodias is the wife of Herod's brother Philip, and John was imprisoned for her sake. She prompts her daughter to ask for John's head on a platter, and the head is brought to her.

l: daughter of Herodias, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Herodias's daughter dances at Herod's birthday and pleases him, so he promises with an oath to give her whatever she asks. Prompted by her mother, she asks for John's head on a platter, receives it, and brings it to her mother.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: At evening the disciples ask Jesus to send the crowds away to buy food, are told to feed them themselves, and distribute the loaves Jesus blesses and breaks, then gather twelve baskets of leftovers. Jesus makes them go ahead by boat, where they are distressed by wind, frightened by the sight of him on the sea, and after he enters the boat they worship him, saying he is truly the Son of God.

l: multitudes (crowds following Jesus), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: The crowds follow Jesus on foot from the cities when he withdraws, and he heals their sick. They sit on the grass and all eat and are filled from the five loaves and two fish, numbering about five thousand men besides women and children. Jesus then sends them away.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Peter asks Jesus to command him to come to him on the waters, and when told "Come!" he steps out of the boat and walks on the water. Seeing the strong wind, he becomes afraid and begins to sink, cries out "Lord, save me!", and Jesus takes hold of him and rebukes him as one of little faith.

l: beheading of John, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Herod, grieved but bound by his oaths and the guests at his table, commands that John's head be given to Herodias's daughter, and John is beheaded in the prison. His head is brought on a platter to the young lady and then to her mother, and John's disciples bury the body and tell Jesus.

l: five loaves for the five thousand, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: With evening come, Jesus has the crowds sit on the grass, takes five loaves and two fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives them to the disciples to distribute. All eat and are filled, about five thousand men plus women and children, and twelve baskets of broken pieces are gathered.

l: boat (disciples' boat), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: Jesus withdraws by boat to a deserted place, and later makes the disciples board a boat to go ahead of him. In the middle of the sea it is distressed by waves and contrary wind; Peter steps out of it, and when Jesus and Peter get into it the wind ceases and those in it worship him.

l: sea, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: The disciples' boat is in the middle of the sea, distressed by waves and a contrary wind, when Jesus comes to them in the fourth watch. Jesus and Peter walk on its waters, and the wind ceases once they are in the boat; afterward they cross over to Gennesaret.

l: Jesus walking on the sea, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 14
s: In the fourth watch of the night Jesus comes to the disciples walking on the sea, and they cry out in fear thinking he is a ghost. He tells them to cheer up and not be afraid, invites Peter to come, and rescues him when he sinks; the wind ceases and the disciples worship him as the Son of God.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem accuse Jesus's disciples of breaking the tradition of the elders by not washing their hands before eating. Jesus answers that they void God's commandment for the sake of their tradition, calls them hypocrites, and teaches the multitude and his disciples that what comes out of the heart, not what enters the mouth, defiles a person. He withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman persistently asks him to heal her demon-possessed daughter, and he grants it because of her faith. Back by the sea of Galilee he heals many lame, blind, mute, and maimed people, then feeds four thousand men plus women and children with seven loaves and a few small fish, with seven baskets left over, before sailing to the borders of Magdala.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: Jesus rebukes the Pharisees and scribes as hypocrites for setting aside God's commandment for their tradition, and teaches that what proceeds from the mouth and heart defiles a person. He heals the Canaanite woman's daughter after testing her with refusals, praising her great faith. He then heals many people by the sea of Galilee, feeds four thousand men plus women and children out of compassion, and sails to the borders of Magdala.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: Pharisees, with scribes, come from Jerusalem and accuse Jesus's disciples of disobeying the tradition of the elders over unwashed hands. Jesus calls them hypocrites and applies Isaiah's prophecy to them. The disciples report that they were offended, and Jesus calls them blind guides of the blind who will fall into a pit.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: The disciples are accused of not washing their hands when they eat bread. They tell Jesus the Pharisees were offended, and Peter asks him to explain the parable, which Jesus does after asking if they still do not understand. They urge Jesus to send the Canaanite woman away, and later doubt that enough bread can be found for the crowd, but they distribute the loaves and fish to the multitudes.

l: God, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: God is the one who commanded honoring father and mother, a commandment the Pharisees' tradition makes void. Jesus calls God his heavenly Father, who will uproot every plant he did not plant. The multitude glorifies him as the God of Israel after seeing the healings.

l: Canaanite woman, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: A Canaanite woman from the borders of Tyre and Sidon cries out to Jesus as Lord and son of David to have mercy on her severely demon-possessed daughter. Despite his silence, the disciples' request to send her away, and his saying that it is not appropriate to give the children's bread to the dogs, she worships him and answers that even dogs eat the crumbs. Jesus praises her great faith, and her daughter is healed from that hour.

l: tradition of the elders, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: The tradition of the elders, which includes washing hands before eating bread, is the basis of the Pharisees' charge against the disciples. Jesus says it leads people to disobey and void God's commandment, and quotes Isaiah that teaching men's rules as doctrine makes worship vain.

l: commandment of God, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: The commandment of God to honor father and mother, with death for whoever speaks evil of them, is cited by Jesus against the Pharisees. He says they make it void through their tradition, allowing a person to declare help owed to parents a gift devoted to God.

l: defilement, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: Jesus teaches that what enters the mouth does not defile a person, since it passes into the belly and out of the body. What proceeds out of the mouth comes from the heart and does defile, namely evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, sexual sins, thefts, false testimony, and blasphemies. Eating with unwashed hands does not defile.

l: multitude, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: Jesus summons the multitude and tells them to hear and understand that what comes out of the mouth defiles. Great multitudes bring the lame, blind, mute, maimed, and others to him, wonder at the healings, and glorify the God of Israel. Having stayed with him three days with nothing to eat, they sit, eat, and are filled, and are then sent away.

l: seven loaves for the four thousand, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 15
s: Out of compassion for the multitude, Jesus takes seven loaves and a few small fish, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to the disciples to distribute. All eat and are filled, and seven baskets of broken pieces are taken up. Those who ate were four thousand men in addition to women and children.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: In Chapter 16 the Pharisees and Sadducees test Jesus by asking for a sign from heaven, and he rebukes them as hypocrites who can read the sky but not the signs of the times, promising only the sign of Jonah. He then warns his disciples about the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees, and they eventually understand he meant their teaching, not bread. At Caesarea Philippi, Simon Peter declares Jesus to be the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus blesses him, calls him Peter, and promises to build his assembly and give him the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven. Jesus then begins to foretell his suffering, death, and resurrection in Jerusalem, rebukes Peter as Satan for objecting, and teaches that following him means denying oneself and taking up a cross, with the Son of Man to come in glory and repay everyone according to their deeds.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: Jesus rebuked the Pharisees and Sadducees for seeking a sign, warned his disciples about their yeast, and asked who people and the disciples said he was. He accepted Peter's confession that he is the Christ, commanded silence about it, and began foretelling his suffering, death, and resurrection. He also taught about denying oneself and said the Son of Man will come in glory and repay each according to deeds.

l: Pharisees, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: The Pharisees, with the Sadducees, tested Jesus by asking for a sign from heaven. Jesus called them hypocrites and an evil and adulterous generation, and warned his disciples against their yeast, which is their teaching.

l: Sadducees, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: The Sadducees came with the Pharisees to test Jesus, asking for a sign from heaven. Jesus rebuked them as part of an evil and adulterous generation and warned his disciples to beware of their teaching, called yeast.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: The disciples forgot to bring bread and misunderstood Jesus's warning about yeast, until he reminded them of the loaves for the five thousand and four thousand and they understood he meant the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. They reported what men say about Jesus, were commanded to tell no one he was the Christ, and were taught that following him requires denying oneself and taking up one's cross.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: Simon Peter answered Jesus's question by declaring him the Christ, the Son of the living God, and was blessed, named Peter, and promised the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven. After Jesus foretold his suffering, Peter took him aside and rebuked him, and Jesus called him Satan and a stumbling block for setting his mind on the things of men.

l: sign from heaven (requested by the Pharisees and Sadducees), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: The Pharisees and Sadducees asked Jesus to show them a sign from heaven to test him. Jesus refused, saying no sign would be given to that evil and adulterous generation except the sign of the prophet Jonah, and then left them.

l: yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: Jesus told his disciples to beware of this yeast, which they first took to be about bread. After Jesus explained, they understood it meant the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

l: Christ, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: Simon Peter declared that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, which Jesus said was revealed by his Father in heaven rather than by flesh and blood. Jesus then commanded the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.

l: assembly (Jesus's assembly), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: Jesus said he will build his assembly on the rock, identified with Peter, and that the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. Peter is promised the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven, with binding and releasing on earth having been bound and released in heaven.

l: Jesus's suffering, death, and resurrection, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: From this time Jesus began showing his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, be killed, and be raised the third day. Peter objected that this would never happen, and Jesus rebuked him.

l: cost of discipleship, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 16
s: Jesus taught that anyone who desires to come after him must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow him. He said whoever tries to save his life will lose it, whoever loses it for his sake will find it, and nothing gained in the world is worth forfeiting one's life.

l: The Gospel According to Matthew, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, where he is transfigured and Moses and Elijah appear; a voice from a cloud declares him the beloved Son. Coming down, Jesus tells the disciples to keep the vision secret until he has risen, and explains that Elijah has already come in the person of John the Baptizer. A man asks Jesus to heal his epileptic son after the disciples failed; Jesus rebukes the demon and cures the boy, then tells the disciples their unbelief was the cause and speaks of mustard-seed faith. Jesus predicts that he will be delivered to men, killed, and raised on the third day. In Capernaum, collectors of the didrachma approach Peter, and Jesus tells him to take a stater coin from a fish's mouth to pay for them both.

l: Jesus, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain, where he is transfigured, his face shining like the sun, and is named by a voice as the beloved Son. He orders silence about the vision until he has risen, heals the boy by rebuking the demon, and predicts his betrayal, death, and third-day raising. In Capernaum he tells Peter to pay the didrachma for both of them with a stater found in a fish's mouth.

l: Peter, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Peter is taken up the mountain with James and John, and offers to make three tents for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah. In Capernaum he tells the didrachma collectors that Jesus pays, and Jesus then sends him to catch a fish holding a stater to pay for them both.

l: Moses, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Moses appears on the high mountain talking with the transfigured Jesus. Peter proposes a tent for him, but afterward the disciples see only Jesus.

l: Elijah, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Elijah appears on the mountain talking with Jesus, and Peter proposes a tent for him. Jesus tells the disciples that Elijah comes first and will restore all things, but has already come and was not recognized, which the disciples understand to mean John the Baptizer.

l: disciples (Jesus's disciples), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Peter, James, and John fall on their faces in fear at the voice from the cloud, and Jesus touches them and tells them to rise. The disciples ask about Elijah, are unable to cure the epileptic boy, and are told it was because of their unbelief. They are exceedingly sorry on hearing Jesus's prediction of his death.

l: voice (from the cloud), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: A voice comes out of a bright cloud that overshadows the mountain. It declares Jesus to be the beloved Son in whom it is well pleased and tells the hearers to listen to him.

l: high mountain (of the transfiguration), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: The high mountain is where Jesus takes Peter, James, and John by themselves. There he is transfigured, Moses and Elijah appear, and the voice speaks from the cloud. The group comes down from it afterward.

l: man (father of the epileptic boy), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: The man kneels before Jesus and asks mercy for his epileptic son, who often falls into fire and water. He explains that he had brought the boy to the disciples, who could not cure him.

l: boy (the man's son), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: The boy is epileptic and suffers grievously, often falling into the fire and the water. Jesus rebukes the demon, it leaves him, and he is cured from that hour.

l: demon (possessing the boy), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: The demon afflicts the boy. Jesus rebukes it, and it goes out of him. Jesus says this kind goes out only by prayer and fasting.

l: faith (as a grain of mustard seed), The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Jesus tells the disciples their failure to cast out the demon was due to unbelief. He says that faith as small as a mustard seed could make a mountain move from here to there, and that nothing would be impossible for them.

l: didrachma collectors, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: The collectors of the didrachma coins come to Peter in Capernaum and ask whether his teacher pays the didrachma. Peter answers yes, and they are later to receive payment from the stater coin Jesus provides.

l: didrachma, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: The didrachma is the coin collected in Capernaum, and the collectors ask whether Jesus pays it. Jesus argues that the children of kings are exempt, but says they will pay anyway so as not to cause stumbling.

l: stater coin, The Gospel According to Matthew, Chapter 17
s: Jesus says Peter will find a stater in the mouth of the first fish he catches with a hook in the sea. Peter is to give it to the collectors for Jesus and himself.
